71.quote_or_event: “O great king, my loving and faithful wife moistened my breast with the tears of her eyes. The poor lady did not eat, nor drink, nor bathe, nor use perfumes, wreaths, and anointment, with my knowledge or without it.”
71.explanation: The monk Anâthin tells King Srenika how, when he lay gravely ill, his wife's love showed itself in tears and in her refusal of food and adornment, though her love could not cure him.
71.tie_back: The kural says love cannot be locked away and shows itself in tears at a loved one's pain; this wife's tears on her sick husband's breast are exactly that.
71._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the image is a strong match, but the lecture uses it to show that human love cannot protect anyone, which is a different point from Valluvar's.

72.quote_or_event: “I will give you my own flesh, weighing it with the dove. Be satisfied. Do not die.”
72.explanation: When a hawk demanded a dove that had fled to his lap, King Megharatha (an earlier birth of the Tîrthankara Shântinâtha) cut off his own flesh to balance the dove on the scales and finally climbed onto the scales himself.
72.tie_back: Megharatha treats his own body as belonging to others, which is precisely Valluvar's picture of the loving, who count even their bones as others' property.
72.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book V (Shântinâthacaritra), ch. IV, part 7, 'Story of the dove and hawk' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS)
72._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a distinctly Jain version of the well-known self-sacrifice motif, and a close match.

73.quote_or_event: “As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to kill. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to tyrannise over. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to torment.”
73.explanation: The Âcârânga teaches that the righteous person sees every other living being's suffering as their own, and for that reason neither kills nor causes others to kill.
73.tie_back: Valluvar says the soul is embodied for the sake of love; the Jain sutra grounds kindness in the soul's recognition of itself in every other embodied being.
73.source: Acaranga Sutra I.5.5.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
73._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. The theme of oneness with other beings fits, but Jainism does not say the soul is embodied for the purpose of love: embodiment is caused by karmic bondage.

74.quote_or_event: “Benevolence (maitrī) towards all living-beings (sattva), joy (pramoda) at the sight of the virtuous (guṇādhika), compassion and sympathy (kāruṇya) for the afflicted (kliśyamāna), and tolerance (mādhyasthya) towards the insolent and ill-behaved (avineya) are the other observances.”
74.explanation: Umâsvâti lists four attitudes to cultivate, starting with maitrî (friendliness toward all beings), and Pûjyapâda's commentary defines pramoda as 'fervent affection' toward the virtuous.
74.tie_back: Valluvar's sequence of love, then warmth toward others, then friendship has a Jain counterpart in maitrî and pramoda, which the sutra presents as cultivated dispositions supporting the vows.
74._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; maitrî corresponds to friendship, but the sutra is a list of contemplations, not Valluvar's causal chain from love to friendship.

75.quote_or_event: “Compassion (anukampā) towards the living-beings (bhūta) in general and the devout (vratī) in particular, charity (dāna), restraint-with-attachment (sarāgasaṃyama), etc., contemplation on the aforementioned, equanimity (kṣānti), and purity (śauca)–freedom-from-greed–lead to the influx (āsrava) of karmas that cause pleasant-feeling (sātā vedanīya).”
75.explanation: In Jain karma theory, compassion and giving draw in the specific karmic matter that later ripens as pleasant experience.
75.tie_back: The kural says the happiness of the fortunate is the fruit of a life settled in love; Umâsvâti says the same in karmic terms, with compassion as the cause of pleasant experience.
75._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a strong doctrinal parallel, although in Jainism even pleasant karma is ultimately a bond to be shed.

76.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, … making Zeal his bow, its string Carefulness in walking, … piercing with the arrow, Penance, (the foe's) mail, Karman--(in this way) a sage will be the victor in battle and get rid of the Samsâra.”
76.explanation: When Indra urges King Nami to build fortifications like a true Kshatriya, Nami turns every military image into a spiritual one: the only war worth fighting is against karma.
76.tie_back: Valluvar says love supports martial valour (maṟam) as much as virtue; Jainism keeps the warrior's courage but points it inward and rejects outward violence.
76._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Jainism's ahimsa conflicts with any endorsement of martial force, so this is a reinterpretation rather than agreement and is scored below 60.

77.quote_or_event: “As the poison Kâlakûta kills him who drinks it; as a weapon cuts him who awkwardly handles it; as a Vêtâla kills him who does not lay him; so the Law harms him who mixes it up with sensuality.” … “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
77.explanation: Speaking of false monks, the sage warns that the Law itself turns against anyone who misuses it, and that the pitiless person is undone by their own nature.
77.tie_back: Valluvar's image of dharma scorching the loveless life as the sun scorches a boneless worm matches this teaching that the Law harms those who abuse it and leaves the man without pity to remorse.
77.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.44 and 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
77._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the idea that dharma itself punishes is a close fit, though the verses are aimed at lapsed monks rather than at lovelessness in general.

78.quote_or_event: “He is empty like a clenched fist, (of no value) like an uncoined false Kârshâpana or like a piece of glass resembling turquoise, he is held lightly by men of discernment.”
78.explanation: An ascetic who keeps the outward forms but neglects vows, penance and self-control is like a hollow fist, a counterfeit coin, or glass passed off as a gem.
78.tie_back: Valluvar's dead tree sprouting in a desert is another picture of apparent life with nothing real behind it, which is what this verse describes.
78._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the image of hollow appearance matches well, but the emptiness here is a lack of discipline rather than a lack of love.

79.quote_or_event: “One does not become a Sramana by the tonsure, nor a Brâhmana by the sacred syllable ôm, nor a Muni by living in the woods, nor a Tâpasa by wearing (clothes of) Kusa-grass and bark. One becomes a Sramana by equanimity, a Brâhmana by chastity, a Muni by knowledge, and a Tâpasa by penance.”
79.explanation: Jayaghosha tells the priest that outward marks make no one holy; only the inner qualities behind them do.
79.tie_back: Valluvar asks what use the outer limbs are without love, the inner organ; this sutra likewise rejects outward marks that lack the inner quality.
79._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the outer-versus-inner structure is close, but the inner quality named is equanimity or knowledge rather than love. Kural 30 drew on other verses of this lecture.

80.quote_or_event: “This body is not permanent, it is impure and of impure origin; it is but a transitory residence (of the soul) and a miserable vessel of suffering. I take no delight in this transitory body which one must leave sooner or later, and which is like foam or a bubble.”
80.explanation: Prince Mrigâputra tells his parents why he will renounce the world: the body is only an impure, temporary lodging of the soul.
80.tie_back: Valluvar says that without love the body is just bones wrapped in skin; the Jain prince shares the view of the bare body as a mere vessel, but finds the remedy in renunciation rather than love.
80._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. The dismissive view of the body is shared, but the Jain reasoning (impermanence and impurity, the ashuchi contemplation) is different from Valluvar's point about love as what animates the body.
